passages.happening:
‘By the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people assembled as one man in Jerusalem’ (verse 1).

Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel, with their fellow priests and associates, begin to build the altar of the God of Israel, ‘as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God’ (verse 2). They set it up on its old foundation and offer the morning and evening burnt offerings to the LORD, ‘even though they feared the people of the land’ (verse 3).

They keep the Feast of Tabernacles, offering burnt offerings each day ‘based on the number prescribed for each day’ (verse 4). The regular offerings begin again, with those for the New Moons and the appointed feasts. And the chapter adds a telling note: ‘On the first day of the seventh month, the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The seventh month, Tishri, falls in September and October. This was probably 538 or 537 BC, the first autumn after the return, and it was the season of Israel's great autumn feasts, so it was natural to gather then.

For about fifty years there had been no regular sacrifice at the temple site in the way the law of Moses commanded. So the first thing the returnees build is not a wall or a house but an altar. By restoring it before anything else, the community says what it is: a people gathered around the worship of the LORD.

The morning and evening burnt offerings were the steady heartbeat of Israel's worship. To restore them was to begin again offering the whole people to God every day.

The Feast of Tabernacles was a seven-day harvest festival in which Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness years. The law set a different number of sacrifices for each of its days, which is what verse 4 means by the number prescribed for each day.

The chapter keeps saying that things were done as the law of Moses had written them (verses 2 and 4). The returnees are careful to do it right. And the two leaders stand for what survived the exile: Jeshua for the priesthood, and Zerubbabel for the house of David. The fear in verse 3 is a small cloud on the horizon. The opposition it hints at will break into the open in chapter 4.
passages.later:
The law of the daily offering said, ‘Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight’ (Exodus 29:39). And the first day of the seventh month was the day of trumpets: ‘This will be a day for you to sound the trumpets’ (Numbers 29:1).

Years later, after Ezra read the law to the people, they kept the Feast of Tabernacles again with great joy: ‘The whole assembly who had returned from exile made booths and lived in them’ (Nehemiah 8:17).
passages.asks: They built the altar first, though they were afraid. Ask what you build first when you start again after a loss. And ask what it would mean in your own life for worship to come before security.

passages.t: Cedar from Lebanon, and the work begins
passages.happening:
The returnees make ready to build. ‘They gave money to the masons and carpenters, and food and drink and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea, as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia’ (verse 7).

‘In the second month of the second year after they had arrived at the house of God in Jerusalem’ (verse 8), Zerubbabel, Jeshua and all who had come back from captivity begin the work. They appoint ‘Levites twenty years of age or older to supervise the construction of the house of the LORD’ (verse 8). Jeshua and his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, and the sons of Henadad, all of them Levites, join together to oversee the workers (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The second month of the second year was probably the spring of 537 or 536 BC.

The preparations deliberately echo Solomon's building of the first temple. Solomon too had paid the people of Tyre and Sidon in food and oil for cedar from Lebanon, floated down the coast. The returnees follow the same route, by sea to the port of Joppa, and then overland to Jerusalem.

The Levites from twenty years old follow the pattern for the temple's workers in Chronicles, and the singers of verse 10 follow the order David had given. This is a community consciously rebuilding on the old foundations, in more than one sense.

And all of it is ‘as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia’ (verse 7). The book never forgets the paperwork. The cedar came by permission.
passages.later:
In Solomon's day, Hiram of Tyre had promised, ‘My servants will haul the logs from Lebanon to the Sea, and I will float them as rafts by sea to the place you specify’ (1 Kings 5:9). Chronicles names the port: ‘we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa’ (2 Chronicles 2:16).

Solomon also began to build in the second month, ‘in the month of Ziv, the second month of the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel’ (1 Kings 6:1).
passages.asks: The returnees built with the same wood, the same road and the same order as their fathers, on the same ground. Ask what you have received from those who went before you that is worth building on again. And ask what part of the work is yours, even if it is only to carry wood.

passages.t: A song of praise, and the sound of weeping
passages.happening:
When the builders had laid the foundation, the priests in their robes, with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, take their places to praise the LORD, ‘as David king of Israel had prescribed’ (verse 10).

‘And they sang responsively with praise and thanksgiving to the LORD’ (verse 11): “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever” (verse 11). All the people give a great shout of praise, because the foundation of the house of the LORD has been laid.

‘But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully’ (verse 12). ‘The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise. And the sound was heard from afar’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The song of verse 11 is a refrain the people knew. It is the refrain of Psalms 106, 107, 118 and 136, and it was sung when the ark came to Jerusalem and when Solomon's temple was dedicated. By using it, the book links this humble beginning to the great moments of Israel's worship.

Loving devotion is the Hebrew chesed: the faithful love that keeps its covenant even with the unfaithful. That is the reason the song gives for the new beginning. Israel had broken faith, but God's chesed endures forever.

The great shout is the Hebrew teruah, the word for a war cry, a trumpet blast, or a loud cry of joy in worship.

Then the weeping. Solomon's temple had been burned about fifty years before, and the oldest people there had seen it standing. To them this foundation looked small. The book does not tell the old men to stop weeping, and it does not tell the young to stop shouting. It ends with both sounds at once, mixed together, and heard far off. Chapter 4 shows who heard it.
passages.later:
The same refrain filled the first temple's dedication: ‘For He is good; His loving devotion endures forever’ (2 Chronicles 5:13).

Some years later the prophet Haggai spoke to the people's disappointment directly: ‘Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How does it look to you now? Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?’ (Haggai 2:3). And he promised, ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former’ (Haggai 2:9). Zechariah asked, “For who has despised the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10).
passages.hard:
Who laid the temple's foundation, and when?

This chapter says the foundation was laid in the second year after the return, under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (verses 8-10), probably 537 or 536 BC. But Ezra 5:16 says that Sheshbazzar laid it. And the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, speaking in 520 BC, describe the foundation as laid in their own day (Haggai 2:18; Zechariah 4:9).

Some scholars think the writer has drawn together work from different periods into this one scene. Others suggest that Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel worked together in the early years, with Sheshbazzar as the official in charge, and that the work of 520 BC was a fresh start on the same foundations after the stoppage told in chapter 4. The Hebrew verb for laying a foundation, yasad, can also mean to restore or repair, which makes both accounts possible.

The chapter's own interest is not the date but the response: an altar first, a song of God's faithful love, and tears beside the shouting.
passages.asks: Some shouted and some wept, and both were heard. Ask whether you can make room, in yourself and in your church, for joy at a new beginning and grief for what has been lost. And ask whether you have looked down on a small beginning because you remember something greater.
